label: a2
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{a2} 
 A forcing notion $\mathbb{Q}$ satisfies $*^\varepsilon_\mu$,
where $\varepsilon$ is a limit ordinal $<\mu$, if Player \textbf{I}
has a winning strategy in the following game:
 
\smallskip\noindent 
 \textbf{Playing}: the play finishes after $\varepsilon$ moves. In the $\alpha^\mathrm{th}$ move:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[Player \textbf{I} --] If $\alpha \ne 0$ he chooses 
    $\langle q_\zeta^\alpha : \zeta < \mu^+\rangle$ such that 
    $q_\zeta^\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}$ and
    $$(\forall\beta<\alpha)(\forall \zeta<\mu^+) [p_\zeta^\beta \le q_\zeta^\alpha]$$ 
    and he chooses a regressive function $f_\alpha : \mu^+ \to \mu^+$ (i.e. $f_\alpha(i) < 1 + i$). 
    If $\alpha = 0$ let $q_\zeta^\alpha = \varnothing_\mathbb{Q}$ and $f_\alpha = \varnothing$.
\smallskip\noindent
    \item[Player \textbf{II} --] He chooses 
    $\langle p_\zeta^\alpha : \zeta < \mu^+\rangle$ such that 
    $q_\zeta^\alpha \le p_\zeta^\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}$.
\end{itemize}

\smallskip\noindent
\textbf{The outcome}: Player \textbf{I} wins provided whenever
$\mu < \zeta < \xi < \mu^+$, $\mathrm{cf}(\zeta) = \mathrm{cf}(\xi) = \mu$, and
$\bigwedge\limits_{\beta<\varepsilon} f_\beta(\zeta) = f_\beta(\xi)$, 
the set $\{p_\zeta^\alpha : \alpha < \varepsilon\} \cup \{p_\xi^\alpha : \alpha < \varepsilon\}$ has an upper bound in $\mathbb{Q}$.

body_md:
\label{a11} 
Suppose $\mu = \mu^{<\mu} < \chi < \lambda$ and $\lambda$ is a 
strongly inaccessible $k_2^2$-Mahlo cardinal, where $k^2_2$ is a
suitable natural number (see \cite[3.6(2)]{Sh:289}), and assume 
$\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{L}$ for simplicity. 

\underline{Then} for some forcing notion $\mathbb{P}$:
\begin{enumerate}[$(A)$]
    \item $\mathbb{P}$ is $\mu$-complete, satisfies the $\mu^+$-c.c., has cardinality $\lambda$, and\\ $\mathbf{V}^\mathbb{P} \models ``2^\mu = \lambda"$.
\smallskip\noindent
    \item $\Vdash_\mathbb{P} \lambda\to [\mu^+]^2_3$ and even
    $\lambda\to[\mu^+]^2_{\kappa,2}$ for $\kappa < \mu$. 
\smallskip\noindent
    \item If $\mu = \aleph_0$ then $\Vdash ``\mathrm{MA}_\chi"$.
\smallskip\noindent
    \item If $\mu > \aleph_0$ \underline{then} $\Vdash_\mathbb{P}$ 
    ``for every $\mu$-complete forcing notion $\mathbb{Q}$ of cardinality $\le\chi$ satisfying $*_\mu^\varepsilon$, and for any dense sets 
    $D_i \subseteq \mathbb{Q}$, for $i < i_0 < \lambda$, there is a 
    directed $G \subseteq \mathbb{Q}$ with 
    $\bigwedge\limits_i G \cap D_i \ne \varnothing$".
\end{enumerate}

body_md:
\label{a20} 
Let $\mu < \chi < \kappa \le \lambda$, $\lambda = \lambda^{<\mu}$,
$\chi = \chi^{<\mu}$, $\mu = \mu^{<\mu}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[1)] We call $x$ a $(\lambda,\kappa,\chi,\mu)$-\emph{pre-candidate} if $x = \langle a^x_u : u \in I_x \rangle$, where for some set $B_x$ (unique, in fact):
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] $I_x = [B_x]^{\leq 2}$                                             
\smallskip\noindent
        \item[(ii)] $B_x$ is a subset of $\kappa$ of order type $\mu^+$.
\smallskip\noindent
        \item[(iii)] $a_u^x$ is a subset of $\lambda$ of cardinality
        $\le\chi$ closed under $\mathrm{Cd}$.
\smallskip\noindent
        \item[(iv)] $a_u^x \cap B_x = u$
\smallskip\noindent
        \item[(v)] $a_u^x \cap a_v^x \subseteq a^x_{u \cap v}$
\smallskip\noindent
        \item[(vi)] If $u,v \in I_x$ and $|u|=|v|$ then $a_u^x$ and $a_v^x$ have the same order type (and so $H^\mathrm{OP}_{a_u^x,a^x_v}$ maps $a_u^x$ onto $a_v^x$).
\smallskip\noindent
        \item[(vii)] If $u_\ell,v_\ell \in I_x$ and 
        $|u_\ell| = |v_\ell|$ for $\ell = 1,2$, 
        $|u_1\cup u_2| = |v_1\cup v_2|$, and 
        $H^\mathrm{OP}_{a^x_{u_1} \cup a^x_{u_2},a^x_{v_1} \cup a^x_{v_2}}$ 
        maps $u_\ell$ onto $v_\ell$ for $\ell=1,2$ then $H^\mathrm{OP}_{a^x_{u_1},a^x_{v_1}}$ and $H^\mathrm{OP}_{a^x_{u_2},a^x_{v_2}}$ are compatible. 
    \end{enumerate}

    \item[2)] We say $x$ is a $(\lambda,\kappa,\chi,\mu)$-candidate if it has the form $\langle M_u^x: u \in I_x\rangle$, where
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(\alpha)$]
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[(i)] $\big\langle |M_u^x| : u \in I_x \big\rangle$ is a $(\lambda,\kappa,\chi,\mu)$-precandidate (with $B_x$ defined as $\bigcup I_x$).
\smallskip\noindent
            \item[(ii)] $\tau_x$ is a vocabulary with $(\le \chi)$-many $(<\mu)$-ary place predicates and function symbols. 
\smallskip\noindent
            \item[(iii)] Each $M_u^x$ is a $\tau_x$-model.
\smallskip\noindent
            \item[(iv)] For $u,\,v\in I_x$ with $|u| = |v|$, $M_u^x\restriction(|M_u^x|\cap|M_v^x|)$ is a model, and in fact an elementary submodel of $M_v^x$, $M_u^x$ and $M^x_{u\cap v}$.
        \end{enumerate}
\smallskip\noindent
        \item[$(\beta)$] For $u,\,v\in I_x$ with $|u| = |v|$, the function $H^\mathrm{OP}_{|M_u^x|,|M_v^x|}$ is an isomorphism from $M_u^x$ onto $M_v^x$.
    \end{enumerate} 

    \item[3)] We say the set $\mathfrak{A}$ is a $(\lambda,\kappa,\chi,\mu)$-\emph{system} if
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(A)] Each $x \in \mathfrak{A}$ is a $(\lambda,\kappa,\chi,\mu)$-candidate.
\smallskip\noindent
        \item[(B)] \textbf{Guessing}: if $\tau$ is as in (2)$(\alpha)$(ii) and $M^*$ is a $\tau$-model with universe $\lambda$, then for some $x\in\mathfrak{A}$, $s\in B_x \Rightarrow M_s^x \prec M^*$.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

\label{a23} 1) We call the system $\mathfrak{A}$ \emph{disjoint} when:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[$(*)$] If $x\ne y$ are from $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathrm{otp}(|M_\varnothing^x|) \le \mathrm{otp}(|M_\varnothing^y|)$ \underline{then} for some 
    $B_1 \subseteq B_x$, $B_2 \subseteq B_y$ we have

        $$\bigcup\{|M_s^x|: s\in [B_x\setminus B_1]^{\le2}\} \text{ and } \bigcup\{|M_s^y|: s\in [B_y\setminus B_2]^{\le2}\}$$
        have intersection $\subseteq M_\varnothing^y$. 
    \end{enumerate}
\end{itemize}
\smallskip\noindent
2) We call the system $\mathfrak{A}$ \emph{almost disjoint} when:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[$(**)$] If $x,\,y\in \mathfrak{A}$ and 
    $\mathrm{otp}(|M_\varnothing^x|) \le \mathrm{otp}(|M_\varnothing^y|)$ \underline{then} for some $B_1\subseteq B_x$ and $B_2\subseteq B_y$ we have:
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item $|B_1|+|B_2| < \mu^+$
\smallskip\noindent
        \item If $s\in [B_x\setminus B_1]^{\le2}$, 
        $t\in [B_y\setminus B_2]^{\le2}$ then $|M_s^x|\cap|M_t^x|\subseteq |M_\varnothing^y|$.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{itemize}

\label{b23} 
Let $d$ be a function with domain $\supseteq [A]^n$, 
$A$ be a set of ordinals, $F$ be a one-to-one 
function from $A$ to ${}^{\alpha(*)}2$, $<_\alpha^*$ be a well 
ordering of ${}^\alpha2$ for $\alpha \le \alpha(*)$ such that 
$F(\alpha)<_\alpha^* F(\beta) \Leftrightarrow \alpha<\beta$, and
$\sigma$ be a cardinal.

\smallskip\noindent
1) We say $d$ is $(F,\sigma)$-\emph{canonical} on $A$ if for any
$\alpha_1 < \ldots < \alpha_n \in A$,
$$\left\vert \big\{ d(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n) : \big\langle F(\beta_1),\ldots,F(\beta_n) \big\rangle \text{ similar to } \big\langle F(\alpha_1),\ldots,F(\alpha_n) \big\rangle \big\}\right\vert\le\sigma$$

\smallskip\noindent
2) We define ``almost $(F,\sigma)$-canonical" similarly using
strongly similar instead of ``similar".

\begin{enumerate}[1)]

Suppose $W = (W,\le)$ is a finite partial order and 
$\mathbf{q} \in \mathfrak{K}$.

\smallskip\noindent
1) $\mathrm{IN}_W(\mathbf{q})$ is the set of $\bar b$-s
satisfying $(\alpha)$--$(\gamma)$ below:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[$(\alpha)$] $\bar b = \langle b_w : w \in W\rangle$ is an 
    indexed set of $\mathbf{q}$-closed subsets of ${\ell\kern-.27ex g}(\mathbf{q})$.
\smallskip\noindent
    \item[$(\beta)$] $W \models w_1 \le w_2 \Rightarrow b_{w_1} \subseteq b_{w_2}$.
\smallskip\noindent
    \item[$(\gamma)$] {If} $\zeta \in b_{w_1} \cap b_{w_2}$, 
    $w_1 \le w$, and $w_2 \le w$ then 
    $$(\exists u\in W)[\zeta \in b_u \wedge u \le w_1 \wedge u \le w_2].$$
\end{enumerate}
We assume $\bar b$ codes $(W,\le)$.

\smallskip\noindent
2) For $\bar b\in \mathrm{IN}_W(\mathbf{q})$, let
$$\mathbf{q}[\bar b] = \big\{\langle p_w : w \in W\rangle : p_w \in
P^\mathrm{cn}_{b_w},\ [W \models w_1 \le w_2\Rightarrow
p_{w_2}\restriction b_{w_1} = p_{w_1}]\big\}$$ with ordering
$\mathbf{q}[\bar b] \models \bar p^1 \le \bar p^2$ iff
$\bigwedge\limits_{w\in W} p^1_w \le p^2_w$.

\smallskip\noindent
3) Let $\mathfrak{K}^1$ be the family of $\mathbf{q} \in \mathfrak{K}$ such 
that for every $\beta \le {\ell\kern-.27ex g}(\mathbf{q})$ and $(\mathbf{q}\restriction\beta )$-closed set $b$, $\mathbb{P}_\beta$ and $\mathbb{P}_\beta / \mathbb{P}^\mathrm{cn}_b$ satisfy the Knaster condition.

body_md:
\label{c26} 
Suppose $\mathbf{q}\in \mathfrak{K}^1$, $(W,\le)$ is a finite partial order, 
$\bar b \in \mathrm{IN}_W(\mathbf{q})$ and $\bar p \in\mathbf{q}[\bar b]$.

\smallskip\noindent
1) If $w\in W$, $p_w \le q \in \mathbb{P}_{b_w}^\mathrm{cn}$ \underline{then} there
is $\bar r \in\mathbf{q}[\bar b]$, $q \le r_w$, $\bar p \le \bar r$. In fact, 
\[
    r_u(\gamma ) =

        p_u(\gamma )\,\, \&\,\, q(\gamma )& \text{if } \gamma\in b_u\cap \mathrm{dom}\ q \text{ and for some } v \in W,\\ 
&\quad u \leq v \le w \text{ and } \gamma\in b_v,\cr
p_u(\gamma)& \text{if } \gamma\in b_u\cap\mathrm{dom}\ q 
        \text{ but the previous case fails.}

\]

\noindent
2) Suppose $(W_1,\le )$ is a submodel of $(W_2,\le )$, both
finite partial orders, $\bar b^l\in \mathrm{IN}_{W_l}(\mathbf{q})$, 
$\bar b^1_w =\bar b^2_w$ for $w\in W_1$. 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[$(\alpha)$] If $\bar q\in\mathbf{q}[\bar b^2]$ then 
    $\langle q_w : w \in W_1\rangle \in\mathbf{q}[\bar b^1]$.
\smallskip\noindent
    \item[$(\beta)$] If $\bar p \in\mathbf{q}[\bar b^1]$ \underline{then} there is $\bar q\in\mathbf{q}[\bar b^2]$ with
    $\bar q\restriction W_1 = \bar p$; in fact, $q_w(\gamma)$ is $p_u(\gamma)$ if $u \in W_1$, $\gamma \in b_u$,and $u \le w$, provided that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(**)$] If $w_1,w_2\in W_1$, $w\in W_2$,
   $w_1\le w$, $w_2\le w$ and $\zeta \in b_{w_1} \cap b_{w_2}$
        then for some $v\in W_1$, $\zeta\in b_v$, $v\le w_1$, $v\le w_2$.
    \end{enumerate}
    (This guarantees that if there are several $u$-s as above we shall get the same value.)
\end{enumerate}

3) If $\mathbf{q}\in\mathfrak{K}^1$ then $\mathbf{q}[\bar b]$ satisfies the

(i.e. $u\in W \Rightarrow W\models \varnothing\le u$)
then $\mathbf{q}[\bar b]/ \mathbb{P}^\mathrm{cn}_{b_\varnothing}$ also satisfies the Knaster

title: Proof
body_md:
) It is easy to check that each $r_u(\gamma)$ is in
$\mathbb{P}^\mathrm{cn}_{b_u}$. So, in order to prove $\bar r\in\mathbf{q}[\bar b]$, 
we assume $W\models u_1\le u_2$ and have to prove that 
$r_{u_2} \restriction b_{u_1} = r_{u_1}$. Let $\zeta\in b_{u_1}$.

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{First case:} $\zeta \notin \mathrm{dom}(p_{u_1}) \cup \mathrm{dom} (q)$. 

So $\zeta \notin \mathrm{dom}(r_{u_1})$ (by the definition of $r_{u_1}$) and
$\zeta \notin \mathrm{dom} (p_{u_2})$ (as $\bar p \in \mathbf{q}[\bar b]$) hence
$\zeta \notin \mathrm{dom} (p_{u_2}) \cup \mathrm{dom}(q)$ hence $\zeta \notin
\mathrm{dom}(r_{u_2})$ by the choice of $r_{u_2}$, so we have finished.

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Second case:} $\zeta\in\mathrm{dom} (p_{u_1})\setminus \mathrm{dom}(q)$.

As $\bar p\in\mathbf{q}[\bar b]$ we have $p_{u_1}(\zeta)=p_{u_2}(\zeta)$,
and by their definition, $r_{u_1}(\zeta)=p_{u_1}(\zeta)$,
$r_{u_2}(\zeta)=p_{u_2}(\zeta)$.

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Third case:} $\zeta\in\mathrm{dom}(q)$ and $(\exists v\in W)$
$[\zeta\in b_v \land v\le u_1\land v\le w]$. 
 
By the definition of $r_{u_1}(\zeta)$, we have 
$r_{u_1}(\zeta)= p_{u_1}(\zeta)\ \&\ q(\zeta)$; also,
the same $v$ witnesses $r_{u_2}(\zeta)=p_{u_2}(\zeta)\ \&\ q(\zeta)$ 
$$(\text{as } \zeta \in b_v \land v \le u_1 \land v \le w \Rightarrow 
                        
 {\zeta \in b_v} \land v \le u_2 \land 
                       
{v \le w}),$$ 
and of course $p_{u_1}(\zeta) = p_{u_2}(\zeta)$ (as
$\bar p\in\mathbf{q}[\bar b]$).

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Fourth case:} $\zeta\in\mathrm{dom}(q)$ and $\neg(\exists v\in
W)[\zeta\in b_v\land v\le u_1 \land v\le w]$. 

By the definition of $r_{u_1}(\zeta)$ we have
$r_{u_1}(\zeta) = p_{u_1}(\zeta)$. It is enough to prove that
$r_{u_2}(\zeta) = p_{u_2}(\zeta)$ as we know that
$p_{u_1}(\zeta) = p_{u_2}(\zeta)$ (because 
$\bar p \in\mathbf{q}[\bar b]$, $u_1 \le u_2)$. If not, then 
for some $v_0 \in W$, $\zeta \in b_{v_0}\land v_0\le u_2 \land v_0\le w$. But $\bar b\in
\mathrm{IN}_W(\mathbf{q})$, hence (see condition
$(\gamma)$ of Definition \ref{c23}(1), applied with $\zeta,\,w_1,\,w_2,\,w$ there standing for
$\zeta,\,v_0,\, u_1,\,u_2$ here) we know that for some $v\in W$,
$\zeta\in v\land v\le v_0\land v\le u_1$. As $(W,\le)$ is a
partial order, $v\le v_0$ and $v_0\le w$, we can conclude $v\le
w$. So $v$ contradicts our being in the fourth case. So we have
finished the fourth case. 

Hence we have finished proving $\bar r\in\mathbf{q}[\bar b]$. We
also have to prove $q\le r_w$, but for $\zeta\in\mathrm{dom}(q)$ we have
$\zeta\in b_w$ (as $q\in \mathbb{P}^\mathrm{cn}_{w}$ is on assumption) and
$r_w(\zeta)=q(\zeta)$ because $r_w(\zeta)$ is defined
by the second case of the definition as 
    $$(\exists v\in W)[\zeta\in b_w\land v\le w \land v\ge w]$$ 
    i.e. $v=w$. 

Lastly, we have to prove that $\bar p\le \bar r$ (in $\mathbf{q}[\bar
b]$). So let $u\in W$, $\zeta \in \mathrm{dom} (p_u)$ and we have to prove
$r_u\restriction \zeta\Vdash_{\mathbb{P}_\zeta}$``$p_u(\zeta)\le_{\mathbb{P}_\zeta} r_u(\zeta)$". As
$r_u(\zeta)$ is $p_u(\zeta)$ or $p_u(\zeta)\; \&\; q(\zeta)$ this is obvious. 

\medskip\noindent
2) Immediate.

3) 
We prove this by induction on $|W|$.

    $A \in [\mu]^\kappa$ and one-to-one $F:A \to {}^\omega 2$ such that $d$ is $F$-canonical on $A$"} (see \S2). 
\smallskip\noindent
    \item[$(*)_3$] If $\lambda \ge \mu \to_\mathrm{wsp}(\aleph_1)^n_{\aleph_2}$ in $\mathbf{V}$ and $d : [\mu]^{\le n} \to \sigma$ in $\mathbf{V}^\mathbb{P}$ (with 
    $\sigma < \aleph_0$) \underline{then}, in $\mathbf{V}^\mathbb{P}$, for every 
    $\alpha < \omega_1$ and $F : \alpha \to {}^\omega 2$, for some

$$i < j < \mu \Rightarrow F^1_{n,m}(u_i) \ne F^1_{n,m}(u_{
                        
{j}}).$$ 
It is easy to check that also $W^1 \mathrel{\vcenter{\baselineskip0.5ex \lineskiplimit0pt\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}= \{F^1_{n,m}(u_i) : i < \mu \}$ 
is a counterexample to $\Pr(\lambda_1,\mu,\sigma)$. In particular, for 
$n,m < \omega$, $W_{n,m} = \{F^1_{n,m}(u):u\in [W]^n\}$ is a 
counterexample if it has power $\mu$. Without loss of generality $W$
is a counterexample with minimal 
$\delta \mathrel{\vcenter{\baselineskip0.5ex \lineskiplimit0pt\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}= \sup(W) = \bigcup\{\alpha + 1 : \alpha \in W\}$.
The above discussion shows that $|W^* \cap \alpha| < \mu$ for $\alpha < \delta$. Obviously $\mathrm{cf}(\delta) = \mu^+$. Let $\langle \alpha_i : i < \mu \rangle$ be a strictly 
increasing sequence of members of $W^*$, converging to $\delta$, 
such that for limit $i$ we have 
$\alpha_i = \min \! \big( W^* \setminus \bigcup\limits_{j<i}(\alpha_j + 1) \big)$. 
Let $N = \bigcup\limits_{i < \mu} N_i$ where $N_i\prec N$, $|N_i| < \mu$, $N_i$ 
increasing continuous, and without loss of generality 
$N_i \cap \delta = N \cap \alpha_i$.

Otherwise we then get an easy contradiction to $\Pr(\lambda_0,\mu,\sigma)$, 
as when choosing the $F^0_{n,m}$ we allowed $\lambda_0$ as a parameter. 
\end{PROOF}

definable in $N$, $F(\alpha)$ is a club of $\alpha$ for every limit
ordinal $\alpha\ (<\lambda_1)$ \underline{then} for some club $C$ of 
$\mu$ we have 
$$\big(\forall j \in C \setminus \{\min C\}\big)
\big(\exists i_1< j\big)\big(\forall i\in (i_1,j)\big)
\big[i\in C\Rightarrow\alpha_i \in F(\alpha_j)\big].$$ 

\begin{PROOF}{\beta}
For some club $C_0$ of $\mu$ we have 
$$j\in C_0 \Rightarrow \big( N_j, \{ \alpha_i : i < j\}, W \big) \prec 
\big(N, \{\alpha_i : i < \mu\}, W \big).$$
We let $C = C'_0 = \mathrm{acc}(C)$ ($=$ set of accumulation points of $C_0$).

We check $C$ is as required; suppose $j$ is a counterexample.
So $j = \sup(j\cap C)$ (otherwise choose $i_1 = \max(j\cap C)$). So we
can define, by induction on $n$, a sequence of $i_n$ such that: 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] $i_n < i_{n+1} < j$
\smallskip\noindent 
    \item[(b)] $\alpha_{i_n} \notin F(\alpha_j)$
\smallskip\noindent 
    \item[(c)] $(\alpha_{i_n},\alpha_{i_{n+1}}) \cap F(\alpha_j) \ne \varnothing $.
\end{enumerate} 

Why $(C'_0)$? $\models$ ``$F(\alpha_j)$ is unbounded below $\alpha_j$" hence
$N\models$ ``$F(\alpha_j)$ is unbounded below $\alpha_j$", but in $N$,
$\{\alpha_i : i\in C_0,\,\,i < j\}$ is unbounded below $\alpha_j$. 

Clearly, for some $n,m$ we have $\alpha_j\in W_{n,m}$ (see above). Now we
can repeat the proof of \cite[3.3(2)]{Sh:276}\footnote{See mainly the end.} using
only members of $W_{n,m}$.\\
Note: here we set the number of colors to be $\aleph_0$.
\end{PROOF}
 
\smallskip\noindent
\textbf{Fact $(\beta)^+$}: Without loss of generality, the club $C$ in Fact $(\beta)$ is $\mu$.

\smallskip\noindent
Proof: By renaming.

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Fact $(\gamma)$}: $\delta$ is a limit cardinal.

\begin{PROOF}{\gamma}
Suppose not. Now $\delta$ cannot be a successor cardinal 
(as $\mathrm{cf}(\delta) = \mu \le \lambda_0 <\delta$) hence for every large enough $i$,
$|\alpha_i| = |\delta|$, so $|\delta| \in W^* \subseteq N$ and
$|\delta|^+\in W^*$. 

So $W^*\cap |\delta|$ has cardinality $<\mu$ hence order-type
equal to some $\gamma^* < \mu$. Choose $i^* < \mu$ limit such that 
$[j < i^* \Rightarrow j + \gamma^* < i^*]$. There is a definable 
function $F$ of\\ $(\mathcal{H}(\chi),\in,<^*_\chi)$ such that for every limit 
ordinal $\alpha$, $F(\alpha)$ is a club of $\alpha$, such that if 
$|\alpha| < \alpha$ then $F(\alpha) \cap |\alpha| = \varnothing$ and
$\mathrm{otp}(F(\alpha)) = \mathrm{cf}(\alpha)$. 

So in $N$ there is a closed unbounded subset $C_{\alpha_j} =
F(\alpha_j)$ of $\alpha_j$ of order type $\le \mathrm{cf}(\alpha_j) \le |\delta|$, hence
$C_{\alpha_j}\cap N$ has order type $\le\gamma^*$, hence for $i^*$
chosen above unboundedly many $i < i^*$, $\alpha_i\notin
C_{\alpha_{i^*}}$. We can finish by Fact $(\beta)^+$. 
\end{PROOF} 
 
\smallskip\noindent
\textbf{Fact $(\delta)$}: For each $i < \mu$, $\alpha_i$ is a
cardinal. 

\begin{PROOF}{\delta}
If $|\alpha_i|<i$ then $|\alpha_i|\in N_i$, but then
$|\alpha_i|^+\in N_i$ contradicting Fact ($\gamma$), by which
$|\alpha_i|^+ <\delta$, as we have assumed $N_i\cap\delta= N\cap\alpha_i$. 
\end{PROOF} 
 
\smallskip\noindent
\textbf{Fact $(\varepsilon)$}: For a club of $i < \mu$,
$\alpha_i$ is a regular cardinal.

\begin{PROOF}{\varepsilon}
If $S = \{i : \alpha_i$ singular$\}$ is stationary, then
the function $\alpha_i \mapsto \mathrm{cf}(\alpha_i)$ is regressive on $S$. 
By Fodor's lemma, for some $\alpha^* <\delta$, 
$\{i < \mu : \mathrm{cf} (\alpha_i) < \alpha^*\}$ is
stationary. As $|N\cap\alpha^*| < \mu$ for some $\beta^*$, 
$\{i < \mu : \mathrm{cf} (\alpha_i) = \beta^*\}$ is stationary. Let $F_{1,m}(\alpha)$ be a
club of $\alpha$ of order type $\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)$, and by Fact ($\beta$) we get
a contradiction as in Fact ($\gamma$). 
\end{PROOF} 

\smallskip\noindent
\textbf{Fact $(\zeta)$}: For a club of $i < \mu$, $\alpha_i$ is Mahlo.

\begin{PROOF}{\zeta}
Use $F_{1,m}(\alpha) =$ a club of $\alpha$ which, if $\alpha$ is
 a successor cardinal or 
inaccessible not Mahlo, then it contains no inaccessible, and
continue as in Fact ($\gamma$). 
\end{PROOF}
 
\smallskip\noindent
\textbf{Fact $(\xi)$}: For a club of $i < \mu$, $\alpha_i$
is $\alpha_i$-Mahlo.

\begin{PROOF}{\xi}
Let $F_{1,m(0)}(\alpha) = \sup\{\zeta:\alpha$ is $\zeta$-Mahlo$\}$.
If the set $\{i < \mu : \alpha_i \text{ is not $\alpha_i$-Mahlo}\}$ is
stationary then as before, for some $\gamma \in N$ we have
$\{i : F_{1,m(0)}(\alpha_i) = \gamma\}$ is stationary. Let
$F_{1,m(1)}(\alpha)$ --- a club of $\alpha$ such 
that if $\alpha$ is not $(\gamma+1)$-Mahlo then the club has no $\gamma$-Mahlo member.
Finish as in the proof of {Fact} $(\delta)$. 
\end{PROOF} 

\smallskip\noindent
Together we are done.

body_md:

$1)$ Suppose $\lambda > \mu > \theta$ are 
regular cardinals, $n\ge 2$, and
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[$(i)$] For every regular cardinal $\kappa$, if $\lambda > \kappa \ge \theta$ then $\kappa \not\to [\theta]^{<\omega}_{\sigma(1)}$.
\smallskip\noindent
    \item[$(ii)$] For some $\alpha(*) < \mu$, for every regular
    $\kappa \in (\alpha(*),\lambda)$, $\kappa \not\to [\alpha(*)]^n_{\sigma(2)}$.
\end{enumerate}
\underline{Then}
\begin{enumerate} 
    \item[$(a)$] $\lambda \not\to [\mu]^{n+1}_\sigma$, where 
    $\sigma = \min\{\sigma(1),\sigma(2)\}$.
\smallskip\noindent
    \item[$(b)$] There are functions $d_2 : [\lambda]^{n+1} \to \sigma(2)$ and
    $d_1 : [\lambda]^3 \to \sigma(1)$ such that for every $W \in [\lambda]^\mu$
    we have $d''_1([W]^3) = \sigma(1)$ or $d''_2([W]^{n+1}) = \sigma(2)$.
\end{enumerate}

\smallskip\noindent 
$2)$ Suppose $\lambda > \mu>\theta$ are regular cardinals, and
\begin{enumerate} 
    \item[$(i)$] For every regular $\kappa \in [\theta,\lambda)$ we have 
    $\kappa \not\to [\theta]^{<\omega}_{\sigma(1)}$. 
\smallskip\noindent
    \item[($ii$)] $\sup\{\kappa < \lambda : \kappa \text{ regular}\} \not\to [\mu]^n_{\sigma(2)}$.
\end{enumerate}
Then
\begin{enumerate} 
    \item[$(a)$] $\lambda\not\to [\mu]^{2n}_\sigma$, where 
    $\sigma = \min\{\sigma(1),\sigma(2)\}$.
\smallskip\noindent
    \item[$(b)$] There are functions $d_1 : [\lambda]^3 \to \sigma(1)$,
    $d_2 : [\lambda]^{2n} \to \sigma(2)$ such that for every 
    $W \in [\lambda]^\mu$ we have $d''_1([W]^3) = \sigma(1)$ or 
    $d''_2([W]^{2n}) = \sigma(2)$.
\end{enumerate}

strictly increasing continuous, and for $i < j < \mu$, 
$\gamma_{i,j} \in [\alpha_i,\alpha_{i+1})$ then 
$$\theta = \big\{d(w) : \hbox{for some } j < \mu,\,\, w \in
\big[\{\gamma_{i,j} : i < j\}\big]^n\big\}.$$
